newsitem.title: KENYA: Flying Kenyan flowers costs less as volume rises.
newsitem.headline: Flying Kenyan flowers costs less as volume rises.

text.p: The cost of flying flowers, fruit and vegetables from Kenya has dropped as more carriers have offered flights in response to booming horticultural production, industry officials said Thursday.

The Kenyan capital of Nairobi is widely regarded as the air-hub of East Africa and the large majority of air cargo come from the horticulture exports of fresh produce. About 90 percent of all horticulture exports are made by by air.

Flowers make up the biggest share of Kenya's total horticulture exports with close to 40,000 tonnes of total exports, while vegetable and fruits account for some 35,000 and some 10,000 tonnes respectively, statistics issued by the Fresh Produce Exporters Association of Kenya (FPEAK) show.

"All flowers, most vegetable and a fairly high percentage of fruits are shipped out by air," said Dr David Grey, an expert in horticulture associated with UK consultants Pathfast Publishing, a group specialised in floriculture trade.
"Although many of the smaller exporting countries are concerned about the lack of airspace, it seems that as production increases so does the number of would-be carriers."

"In Kenya the freight rate has dropped over the past three years from $2.15 per kilogramme to $1.70 per kilogramme," Grey told a seminar at Kenya's annual horticulture exhibition, the three-day Hortec '97 which is the biggest such trade exhibition in sub-Saharan Africa.
"In volume terms fresh horticulture exports recorded 57,364 metric tonnes in 1992, rising to 71,758 tonnes in 1995," said, FPEAK chairman Simon Ethangatta.
"1996 has done even better with a record high of 84,824 tonnes, a 18.2 percent increase in volume over 1995 exports," Ethangatta said in his opening remarks.
Horticulture exports in 1995 was worth $193 million in foreign exchange earnings, but 1996 figures were not available.
He said latest statistics from the flower auctions in Holland showed a clear increase in exports to the markets in Russia and Eastern Europe, while new markets were showing up all over the world.
Grey also said that especially exports of cut flowers to the European market in the last few years had been dominated by production from emerging developing countries in Africa.

"Our statistics still largely ignore another increasingly important area for our trade, Russia and Eastern Europe. Neither should the Far East markets such as Taiwan, China and Korea be ignored...particularly in cut flowers and foliage."

"Most of the future expansions in the interantional trade will come from newer consuming countries as they open up their borders. For instance, Russia and Eastern Europe are beginning to import appreciable numbers of flowers and plants," Grey said.
He said that while imports of cut flowers to Europe had almost doubled in the last 12 years, exports from Africa to Europe had increased eight fold.
International trade of cut flowers in 1996 increased to $3.15 billion worth of sales, up from $2.71 billion in 1995, a growth of 16 percent, Grey said.
"The most dramatic change in the last few years has been the emergence of Africa, particularly East and Central Africa, as the major supplier area to the European market.

"There has been a realisation in many of the developing countries as to the potential benefits of the floriculture trade to their economies. Developed countries such as Israel, Colombia and Morocco are finding that they are losing market share, especially to countries with lower production costs such as Kenya, Zimbabwe, Costa Rica and Ecuador," Grey concluded.

The majority of Kenya's horticulture exports, about 32 percent, are shipped to the Netherlands, while the UK market accounts for about 28 percent. The remaining exports are for the large majority shipped to other European markets, according to FPEAK. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+5017
